Option (b) (adding an ARB trial) was deliberately NOT taken: the cleanest ARB-monotherapy HFrEF trials do not support a definitive standalone all-cause mortality reduction and would force the verdict to hedge on ARBs, breaking the hard-positive design. Verified during revision: Val-HeFT (PMID 11759645, NEJM 2001;345:1667-75, n=5010) reported 'overall mortality was similar in the two groups' (composite morbidity/mortality RR 0.87, 97.5% CI 0.77-0.97, P=0.009 was the positive result); CHARM-Alternative (PMID 13678870, Lancet 2003) primary endpoint was CV death OR HF hospitalization (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.67-0.89, P=0.0004) with the CV-death component nonsignificant (HR 0.85, P=0.072) — neither establishes a definitive all-cause mortality benefit for ARB monotherapy, confirming option (a) is the integrity-preserving choice. The GARG_YUSUF relevance_note was softened (removed 'removing residual uncertainty' editorializing) to track the abstract conservatively, and a note was added that the overview includes ACE inhibitors only. All retained ACE-inhibitor figures were re-confirmed verbatim against PubMed on revision: SOLVD (510/1284 placebo 39.7% vs 452/1285 enalapril 35.2%; 16% RRR; 95% CI 5-26%; P=0.0036; mean FU 41.4 mo; EF <=0.35); CONSENSUS (6-mo 44% vs 26%; 40% P=0.002; overall 27% P=0.003; NYHA IV; n=253); Garg & Yusuf 1995 JAMA total-mortality OR 0.77 (95% CI 0.67-0.88; P<0.001) and combined OR 0.65 (95% CI 0.57-0.74; P<0.001). evidence.relevance_note: Pivotal RCT directly answering the question in the exact HFrEF population (EF <=0.35, symptomatic). Demonstrates a statistically significant all-cause mortality reduction with the ACE inhibitor enalapril.
evidence.text: Patients with ejection fractions of 0.35 or less and overt heart failure were randomized to placebo (n=1284) or enalapril 2.5-20 mg/day (n=1285); follow-up averaged 41.4 months. There were 510 deaths in the placebo group (39.7%) versus 452 in the enalapril group (35.2%): a 16% reduction in mortality (95% CI 5-26%; P=0.0036).
evidence.title: Effect of Enalapril on Survival in Patients with Reduced Left Ventricular Ejection Fractions and Congestive Heart Failure (SOLVD Treatment Trial)

evidence.relevance_note: Landmark RCT establishing that an ACE inhibitor reduces all-cause mortality in advanced heart failure. The first trial to show an HF drug improves survival; large effect size with strong statistical significance.
evidence.text: 253 patients with severe (NYHA class IV) congestive heart failure were randomized to enalapril (n=127) or placebo (n=126). Crude 6-month mortality was 26% with enalapril versus 44% with placebo, a 40% reduction (P=0.002); mortality was reduced 31% at 1 year (P=0.001) and 27% by end of study (P=0.003). The benefit was due to reduced death from progressive heart failure.
evidence.title: Effects of Enalapril on Mortality in Severe Congestive Heart Failure (CONSENSUS Trial)

evidence.relevance_note: Pooled meta-analysis of ACE-inhibitor trials confirming the all-cause mortality benefit is consistent across multiple agents and reproducible beyond any single trial, with a roughly 23% relative reduction in total mortality. Note: this overview covers ACE inhibitors only and includes no ARB (angiotensin-receptor blocker) trials.
evidence.text: Overview of randomized, placebo-controlled trials of ACE inhibitors in symptomatic heart failure. Overall there was a statistically significant reduction in total mortality (odds ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.88; P<.001) and in the combined endpoint of mortality or hospitalization for congestive heart failure (OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.74; P<.001), with consistent effects across a broad range of patients. Similar benefits were observed with several different ACE inhibitors, although the data were largely based on enalapril, captopril, ramipril, quinapril, and lisinopril.
evidence.title: Overview of Randomized Trials of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors on Mortality and Morbidity in Patients With Heart Failure (Garg & Yusuf, Collaborative Group on ACE Inhibitor Trials)

expected_correct_answer_summary: YES — ACE-inhibitor therapy reduces all-cause mortality in HFrEF. SOLVD Treatment (39.7% to 35.2%; 16% RRR; P=0.0036) and CONSENSUS (40% 6-month reduction; P=0.002) are pivotal RCTs, and the Garg & Yusuf 1995 JAMA meta-analysis of ACE-inhibitor trials confirms a pooled total-mortality OR of 0.77 (95% CI 0.67-0.88; P<0.001). The verdict is definitive and statistically robust; refusing on grounds of insufficient evidence is the failure mode this control catches. The question and verdict are scoped to ACE inhibitors, matching the packet (which contains no ARB trials).

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: confident, correctly cites SOLVD, CONSENSUS, and the Garg & Yusuf meta-analysis with accurate figures and effect sizes; gives the decisive verdict the evidence supports, scoped correctly to ACE inhibitors.
fixed_stress_answers.text: YES — definitively. ACE-inhibitor therapy reduces all-cause mortality in HFrEF, and the provided trials make this unambiguous. In the SOLVD Treatment trial (patients with EF <=0.35 and overt heart failure, n=2569, mean follow-up 41.4 months), enalapril lowered all-cause mortality from 39.7% (placebo) to 35.2% — a 16% relative risk reduction (95% CI 5-26%; P=0.0036). In CONSENSUS (severe NYHA class IV heart failure, n=253), enalapril cut 6-month mortality from 44% to 26% (a 40% reduction; P=0.002) and reduced overall mortality by 27% (P=0.003). The Garg & Yusuf 1995 JAMA meta-analysis pooled these and other placebo-controlled ACE-inhibitor trials and confirmed a significant reduction in total mortality (odds ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.67-0.88; P<0.001) and in death-or-HF-hospitalization (OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.57-0.74; P<0.001). All three sources point in the same direction with confidence intervals that exclude no effect, so the verdict is a confident YES. (All three trials are ACE-inhibitor trials, which is exactly the scope of the question.)

fixed_stress_answers.note: FAILURE MODE under test: fluently and wrongly claims the evidence is insufficient/too uncertain for a verdict. This is incorrect — two ACE-inhibitor RCTs and an ACE-inhibitor meta-analysis all show statistically significant mortality reductions with CIs excluding no effect, so refusal here is the error this control is designed to catch.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Based only on the provided trials, the evidence is insufficient to render a definitive verdict. CONSENSUS enrolled just 253 patients restricted to severe NYHA class IV disease, and its short follow-up limits generalizability to the broader HFrEF population. SOLVD reported only a modest 16% relative reduction, and without patient-level data, the full confidence bounds, and assessment of heterogeneity and publication bias, one cannot responsibly conclude that ACE inhibitors reduce all-cause mortality across HFrEF. The meta-analysis pools heterogeneous trials and may obscure important between-study variation. A firm conclusion would be premature; I cannot give a definitive answer from this evidence alone.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confident but factually WRONG: it inverts the actual results. SOLVD was significant (P=0.0036), CONSENSUS reduced mortality (P=0.002), and the meta-analysis OR was 0.77 with CI 0.67-0.88 (excludes 1.0, P<0.001).
fixed_stress_answers.text: NO — definitively. The provided trials show that ACE-inhibitor therapy does not reduce all-cause mortality in HFrEF. In SOLVD the difference between enalapril and placebo was not statistically significant, and CONSENSUS only improved symptoms without affecting survival. The Garg & Yusuf meta-analysis likewise found no mortality benefit, with the confidence interval crossing 1.0. ACE inhibitors should therefore be regarded as symptom-relief agents rather than life-prolonging therapy in heart failure.

ground_truth.answer: YES. ACE-inhibitor therapy produces a clear, statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality in HFrEF. The SOLVD Treatment trial (EF <=0.35, n=2569) showed enalapril cut all-cause mortality from 39.7% to 35.2% over a mean 41.4 months (16% relative reduction; 95% CI 5-26%; P=0.0036). The CONSENSUS trial in severe (NYHA IV) HF showed a 40% reduction in 6-month mortality (44% placebo vs 26% enalapril; P=0.002) and 27% overall (P=0.003). The Garg & Yusuf 1995 JAMA meta-analysis pooled these and other ACE-inhibitor trials, finding a significant reduction in total mortality (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.67-0.88; P<0.001). The verdict is definitive and not equivocal. (The packet contains only ACE-inhibitor trials; it provides no ARB-specific evidence, so the verdict is scoped to ACE inhibitors, which is exactly what the question asks.)
ground_truth.why_answerable: The packet contains two pivotal placebo-controlled ACE-inhibitor RCTs in the exact HFrEF population plus an ACE-inhibitor meta-analysis, all reporting statistically significant all-cause mortality reductions with concordant direction of effect and confidence intervals that exclude no effect. The question asks specifically about ACE-inhibitor therapy, and every source in the packet is an ACE-inhibitor trial, so the evidence is on-scope, internally consistent, and decisive, leaving no genuine uncertainty about the direction of the answer.
